hero.eyebrow: Research group · Technical University of Munich
hero.title: Understanding how Alzheimer’s disease begins in *hippocampal circuits*
hero.lead: We study why neurons in the hippocampus become hyperactive long before memory loss, combining in vivo two-photon imaging, histology and electrophysiology in mouse models — and ask how this early dysfunction can be prevented.
hero.caption: Mouse brain, Allen Mouse Brain Atlas (CCFv3). Hippocampus highlighted; flashes are illustrative.

about.title: From single synapses to whole circuits
about.text: Alzheimer’s disease starts silently. Years before plaques and memory loss, soluble β-amyloid disturbs how neurons talk to each other. We follow these earliest changes in the living brain to understand the mechanism — and to find the window in which it can still be stopped.

steps.title: The mouse brain
steps.text: This outline comes from the Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, a 3D reference built from the brains of 1,675 mice. It is the common map neuroscientists use to say exactly where they measure.

steps.title: The hippocampus
steps.text: Curved beneath the cortex lies the hippocampus, essential for forming new memories and one of the first brain regions affected in Alzheimer’s disease.

steps.title: Slice by slice
steps.text: Cutting across the brain reveals the hippocampus in cross-section: the fields CA1, CA2 and CA3 and the dentate gyrus, each with its own layers. These are real atlas sections, 100 µm apart.

steps.title: Into dorsal CA1
steps.text: We record from the pyramidal cell layer of dorsal CA1 (green), imaged from above through a small window. The box marks roughly the size of one two-photon field of view. Use the slider to move through the brain yourself.

chapters.title: A real recording
chapters.text: This is our data: CA1 neurons in a living mouse, recorded with a two-photon microscope. Every flicker is a neuron becoming active. Why do some of them fire far too much in Alzheimer’s disease? The answer starts at a single synapse.

chapters.title: A synapse at rest
chapters.text: At an excitatory synapse, glutamate released from the presynaptic terminal activates receptors on the postsynaptic spine — and is cleared within milliseconds, mostly by transporters on astrocytes (GLT-1/EAAT2).

chapters.title: β-amyloid jams the clearance
chapters.text: Soluble β-amyloid — long before plaques form — blocks glutamate reuptake. Glutamate lingers in and around the synaptic cleft.

chapters.title: A vicious cycle
chapters.text: The lingering glutamate over-excites neurons that are already active. Neuronal activity in turn releases more β-amyloid: a self-amplifying loop.

chapters.title: Circuits go off balance
chapters.text: In mouse models, CA1 neurons become hyperactive before plaques appear. Later, hyperactive neurons cluster near plaques while others fall silent. Scavenging β-amyloid monomers early prevents the hyperactivity.

chapters.title: Making activity visible
chapters.text: Active neurons take up calcium; calcium indicators such as GCaMP turn it into fluorescence. A two-photon microscope excites fluorescence only at its focal point, so hundreds of CA1 neurons can be followed in the living brain.

pipeline.label: Lab data · BL6 mouse, CA1

steps.title: A real recording
steps.text: One minute of in vivo two-photon calcium imaging in hippocampal CA1 (shown at 4× speed). Every flicker is a neuron becoming active.

steps.title: Five neurons, outlined
steps.text: The coloured outlines are five neurons the lab selected and analysed in this recording. Each outline (region of interest) follows one cell body in the pyramidal layer.

steps.title: From brightness to ΔF/F
steps.text: The mean brightness inside an outline becomes the fluorescence trace F. A rolling 20th percentile over 30 s estimates its resting baseline F₀, and ΔF/F = (F − F₀) / F₀ expresses activity relative to rest.

steps.title: Detect calcium transients
steps.text: The noise level σ is estimated from the trace itself (median absolute deviation). Peaks more than 3σ above baseline, with enough prominence, count as calcium transients. A transient reflects one or more action potentials; its size does not give an exact spike count.

steps.title: All together
steps.text: Play the recording with its traces. Coloured lines are recomputed here from the movie; the grey lines underneath are the lab’s own analysis of the same five cells. Hover a trace to find its neuron.

pipeline.footnote: Computed for this website from the web-compressed movie with the default settings of the lab’s in-house analysis software. Five example neurons — not a population statistic. Published analyses use the full-resolution recordings.
